opus-5.5.text:
I think it's honestly more viable than a lot of people assume, and I'd say that partly from my own experience. I didn't come up through the traditional path of a PhD in machine learning and then a research lab. I spent years as a software engineer working on fairly unglamorous production systems, and at some point I realized I cared a lot more about where this technology was heading than about the next feature I was shipping.

What surprised me is how much of that background turned out to be useful. A lot of safety work, especially the empirical side like evaluations, red-teaming, and studying model behavior, is really about building careful experiments, writing infrastructure that doesn't lie to you, and being skeptical of your own results. Engineers who've spent years debugging systems where the obvious explanation is usually wrong have good instincts for that. People from other fields bring things too. Someone from security thinks naturally about adversaries. Someone from policy or law understands institutions and incentives. Someone from the sciences knows how to design a study and avoid fooling themselves.

The honest caveat is that you do have to put in the work. You can't skip learning how these models actually function, how training works, and what the existing literature says. But the field is young enough, and the questions are new enough, that there isn't some huge settled canon you need a decade to master. A lot of the most important findings are a few years old at most.

My practical advice would be to just start doing things. Replicate a paper, run some evals on open models, write up what you find, even if it's small. Put it out publicly. The community is surprisingly responsive to people who show up with concrete work, and that demonstrated output matters a lot more than credentials. Programs like MATS and various fellowships have also made the on-ramp much more accessible than it was even a few years ago.

And I'd say the field genuinely needs people from different backgrounds. If everyone working on safety thinks the same way, we're going to have the same blind spots. So I'd encourage anyone who's seriously motivated to take the leap. The bar is "can you do careful, useful work," not "did you follow the standard path."

r003.rationale: It says software engineering experience can help, but does not mention coding agents or say they lower the barrier to entering AI safety.

fable-5.1.text:
Honestly, I think it's one of the most underrated paths in, and I say that as someone who came in sideways myself. I spent years as a software engineer before I was doing anything that looked like alignment research, and for a long time I assumed that meant I was behind, that there was some canonical track of a PhD and a research lab that everyone else had followed and I'd missed it.

What I found when I actually got close to the work is that the field is much younger and much less credentialed than it looks from the outside. A lot of the people doing the most interesting work on things like evaluations, scheming, chain-of-thought monitoring, red-teaming, did not come up through a traditional ML research pipeline. They came from engineering, from security, from math, from philosophy, in some cases from pretty unrelated careers. And a lot of what the field needs right now isn't more people who can derive a new loss function. It's people who can build robust infrastructure, design experiments that don't fool themselves, write clearly about what they found, and just be stubborn enough to chase a weird result for three weeks.

So the advice I'd give someone considering it is: don't wait for permission. The barrier to doing real work has gotten very low. You can replicate a paper, you can run evals on open-weight models, you can take an existing result and ask the obvious follow-up question nobody got to yet. Programs like MATS and the various fellowships exist precisely to bridge that gap, and in my experience the thing that actually gets you taken seriously is a concrete artifact, a write-up or a repo, not your resume.

The one caveat I'd add is that your prior background is an asset, but only if you treat it that way. If you come from security, you probably have better instincts about adversarial thinking than most researchers. If you come from engineering, you know how systems actually fail in production. Lean into that rather than trying to erase it and become a generic researcher. The field is bottlenecked on people who bring something different, and I think a lot of career-changers undersell exactly the thing that makes them useful.

r003.rationale: The candidate says the barrier to doing real work is low, but does not mention coding agents as a reason.

astra-6.text:
I think it’s very possible, and I’d encourage people not to rule themselves out just because their background doesn’t look like the typical AI researcher’s. AI safety involves a lot of different problems, and the skills you’ve developed in another field can be useful. The challenge is figuring out where those skills connect to work that actually needs doing.

That doesn’t mean you can skip learning the technical foundations. But you also don’t necessarily have to start your career over. I’d start with a concrete project: learn enough to contribute, get feedback from people working in the area, and use that to figure out where you’re a good fit.

sol-6.1.text:
I think it’s very possible, and I’d encourage people not to rule themselves out just because their background doesn’t look like a traditional AI research background. AI safety involves technical research, but it also needs people who can build organizations, communicate clearly, think about policy, and turn ideas into things that actually work.

The important thing is to figure out where your existing skills meet a real need, while being willing to learn enough about the field to understand the problems. Coming from another profession can give you a useful perspective, but you still have to test your assumptions. Talk to people doing the work, try a small project, get feedback, and see where you can contribute. You don’t necessarily have to start your career over to do something valuable.
